context: Current closing price of Chipotle (CMG): $35.17 USD as of 2026-11-12.
justification_text:
My point estimates across all horizons – one day, one week, and one month – consistently settled at 35.17 because this value represented my best assessment of the underlying state of the system being forecasted. It suggested that, based on the information available at the time, 35.17 was the most stable and probable outcome, acting as a baseline or an expected average around which future observations would fluctuate. There was no discernible trend or immediate catalyst identified that would systematically push the value higher or lower over these specific timeframes, indicating a belief in the short-to-medium term stability of this central value.

The expanding width of the confidence intervals, however, directly reflects the increasing uncertainty inherent in forecasting further into the future. For the one-day horizon, the narrow interval accounts mostly for minor random fluctuations and very short-term noise. As the forecast extends to one week and then one month, the range widens considerably. This broader uncertainty stems from several factors, including the accumulation of everyday variability, potential for minor model inaccuracies to compound over time, and the growing possibility of small, unpredictable events that can nudge the outcome further from the central estimate. Essentially, while the central tendency remains constant, our confidence in the exact future value diminishes as the prediction window extends.

Beyond the expected variability captured within these confidence intervals, specific high-impact events or unforeseen circumstances could push the actual outcome well outside the stated ranges. These include significant and sudden policy changes by governments or central banks, major economic shocks such as an unexpected recession or a rapid inflationary surge, or unpredictable geopolitical developments like conflicts or trade wars. Furthermore, substantial technological disruptions, large-scale natural disasters, or unprecedented shifts in market demand or supply could also fundamentally alter the underlying dynamics. These "tail risks" are by their nature difficult to predict or quantify within a standard probabilistic model, but their likelihood, while low, incrementally increases over longer time horizons, making them more relevant to the one-month forecast than to the immediate one-day outlook.
